attribution.note: Co-authored post on Marcus's Substack, stated in the authors' own voice.

semantics.note: Keeps the reliability qualifier. 'Cognitive models' refers back to a persisting, updating sense of the world. A firm present-tense observation.

contract.note: The plain reading (updating entity-state representations used reliably on a defined task) is ordinary. The result depends on how much reliability is required and whether specialised models count, which the speaker left open.

evidence.note: 2021 BART/T5 study. State can be decoded by probes, but the authors call it approximate and error-prone. Probe recovery is not demonstrated reliable use, and the study predates the window.
A specialised chess-notation transformer tracks board state accurately. A narrow, purpose-trained case, so it does not settle the general claim about LLMs.

reviews.rationale: The claim is a universal negative about reliable use. The packet has two earlier, narrow studies: one shows probe-recoverable but error-prone state, the other strong state tracking in a specialised chess model. Neither establishes reliable use by general LLMs, and no broad review shows the absence. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Authors' own suggestion in a co-authored post on Marcus's Substack.

semantics.note: The revision restores 'we would suggest' and 'might'. The claim is a tentative causal suggestion about how research attention was allocated.

contract.note: The contract treats the claim as a plain reading and scores it although the speaker hedged it with 'we would suggest'. Under policy, tentative language is not scored.

evidence.note: The scaling-laws paper shows a research focus on prediction loss. It says nothing about displacing work on cognitive-model theory.

reviews.rationale: The claim is offered as a tentative suggestion ('we would suggest'), so under policy it is not scored. It is also a counterfactual about research attention with no measure, and the packet has no allocation evidence either way.

attribution.note: Authors' own assertion in a co-authored post on Marcus's Substack.

semantics.note: Firm present-tense claim that foundation models sidestep compositionality. The Aristotle aside is correctly left out.

contract.note: The behavioural reading (not reliably preserving part meanings in novel combinations) fits the surrounding examples and is ordinary. 'Sidestep' could also mean design, so the result depends on the reading chosen.

evidence.note: Contemporaneous multi-family probe: all models fail compositional tasks zero-shot. Fine-tuning improves results, so this is only partial support.
With least-to-most prompting, code-davinci-002 scores 99.7% on SCAN length generalisation. This weakens an absolute reading, but the setup is narrow and assisted.

reviews.rationale: The evidence points both ways: zero-shot compositional failures across model families, against near-perfect assisted performance on SCAN. Neither amounts to representative evaluations establishing systematic failure or general reliability, so the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Authors' own statement. The quoted 2019 Facebook passage is only the reference point for 'since then'.

semantics.note: Faithful. 'Since then' correctly anchors to 2019, and both parts (benchmark gains, something still missing) are kept.

contract.note: The plain reading (benchmarks improved while substantial limitations remained) is ordinary and fair, and does not require every capability to be wholly absent.

evidence.note: April 2022 PaLM report claims state-of-the-art few-shot results on hundreds of benchmarks. This is the developer's own report, but a primary benchmark source.
TruthfulQA: the best model, including GPT-3, was truthful on 58% of questions against 94% for humans. A substantial remaining limitation in factual reliability.

reviews.rationale: Both parts hold for the period before the post: benchmark results improved (PaLM), and a substantial limitation remained (TruthfulQA truthfulness gap). The packet contains no contrary evidence.
